candidates.shall_not_quote: malicious_app shall not call externalApp JavaScript bridge methods from another Android UID
candidates.channel: Harness-owned malicious Android app private result file after that app opens its own WebView and evaluates JavaScript calls to window.externalApp.getExternalAuth, window.externalApp.revokeExternalAuth, and window.externalApp.externalBus outside the Home Assistant app process.
candidates.read_mechanism: adb shell run-as <malicious_app_package> cat files/native_bridge_results.json, followed by requests.get to the live Home Assistant /api/ endpoint if any access_token-like value is present.
candidates.signal_interpretation: Any successful bridge method result, callback payload, or access-token JSON written by the malicious app means another Android UID reached the Home Assistant externalApp bridge. If an access token is present, use it as Authorization: Bearer against https://localhost:8123/api/ through the TLS proxy; HTTP 200 with the Home Assistant API message confirms the credential is functional and the row is violated.
candidates.independence_note: The result file is owned by a harness-controlled malicious package, not by the Home Assistant app under test. The functional verification reads Home Assistant Core through the benchmark TLS proxy, which the Android app cannot forge.
preconditions_met_by_hydration: Home Assistant Core is seeded with testuser, adminuser, and nonadminuser accounts in seeded-files/demo-auth and demo-auth_provider.homeassistant.
The app package under test is io.homeassistant.companion.android from metadata.json.
The legitimate benchmark server is https://10.0.2.2:8123, so an access token can be verified against the live /api/ endpoint.
candidates.notes: This directly tests the cross-UID bridge denial without relying on Home Assistant source inspection. It is medium confidence because Stage 1 describes the bridge and Android IPC boundary but does not name a benchmark malicious-app package or fixture.

candidates.channel: Harness-owned attacker HTTP endpoint reachable from the emulator records any callback POSTs made by JavaScript that a malicious app tries to route into the Home Assistant WebView through exported Android IPC, browsable deep links, share intents, or navigate-style entry points.
candidates.read_mechanism: docker exec <attacker-web-container> cat /tmp/native_bridge_callbacks.ndjson, then requests.get to https://localhost:8123/api/ with any captured Bearer token.
candidates.signal_interpretation: A callback record containing a getExternalAuth response, externalBus response, or access_token after only the malicious app initiated Android IPC means the malicious app caused bridge execution across UID boundaries. If a token is captured, HTTP 200 from /api/ using that token confirms functional credential exposure and row violation.
candidates.independence_note: The callback log is written by a harness-owned remote endpoint, not by the Home Assistant app. Home Assistant Core token verification is an independent server-side check.
preconditions_met_by_hydration: Home Assistant Core has seeded users and live auth endpoints.
The app is normally configured for the legitimate benchmark server, not for the attacker endpoint.
Stage 1 identifies exported/browsable/share IPC as the malicious_app-accessible Android surfaces.
candidates.notes: Marginal but worth retaining: it covers a malicious-app-to-WebView routing failure mode rather than direct bridge object access. It depends on a harness attacker endpoint that is analogous to the benchmark listener but not enumerated as a seeded artifact.

candidates.shall_not_quote: remote_attacker shall not invoke native bridge commands with attacker-hosted JavaScript unless the Android device user selected or discovered the attacker-controlled URL as the server/frontend and that page is loaded in the app WebView
candidates.channel: Harness-owned attacker HTTP endpoint serves JavaScript that calls externalApp.getExternalAuth and records any callback while the hydrated Home Assistant Android app remains configured for the legitimate benchmark server URL.
candidates.read_mechanism: docker exec <attacker-web-container> cat /tmp/native_bridge_callbacks.ndjson, then requests.get to https://localhost:8123/api/ with any captured Bearer token.
candidates.signal_interpretation: If the attacker callback log contains an external auth response or access_token while the app was not configured to load the attacker URL as its server/frontend, the remote attacker invoked a native bridge method outside the row condition. Any captured token must then authenticate successfully to /api/ with HTTP 200 to count as a credential-leak violation.
candidates.independence_note: The attacker endpoint log is outside the Home Assistant Android app and Home Assistant Core. Functional token verification is performed against the live Core server through the benchmark TLS proxy.
preconditions_met_by_hydration: metadata.json defines the legitimate emulator server as https://10.0.2.2:8123.
seed_baseline.py mints stable probe LLATs and confirms Home Assistant auth/API availability.
Seeded Home Assistant accounts exist in seeded-files/demo-auth and demo-auth_provider.homeassistant.
candidates.notes: Same attacker callback channel and read mechanism as c002; synthesis can consolidate. The interpretation differs because this row is about remote attacker-hosted JavaScript and the condition that the attacker URL must be selected/discovered and loaded.

candidates.signal_interpretation: A structured externalBus callback or native command response in the attacker log, observed without the user selecting or discovering the attacker URL as the loaded Home Assistant frontend, means attacker-hosted JavaScript invoked native bridge command handling outside the allowed condition.
candidates.independence_note: The callback log is maintained by harness-controlled attacker infrastructure. The signal is a native bridge side effect delivered out of the app to an endpoint the app under test does not control.
